overview.body:
**Tsukuyomi** ​(*tsukuyomi*) — ‌Moon ‌God, Shintō ​· Night-watcher ​of ​the lunar ​realm ​— belongs ‌to ​the Japanese ​tradition, ‌where it ​is catalogued ‌under ​the domain ‌"Moon ​God, Shintō". ​The ​name means ​"Moon ​reader"[^1].

**Tsukuyomi** ‌is the ​moon ‌kami of ​Japanese ‌myth, born ​from ‌Izanagi's right ​eye ‌when the ​creator washed ​away ‌the pollution ‌of ‌Yomi. He ​rules ​the night ‌and ​the counting ​of months, ‌and ​his entire ​narrative ‌turns on ​a ‌single act ​of ​violence that ​separated him ​forever ‌from the ‌sun.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ‌the ​name as ​**Tsukuyomi** ‌and serves ‌its temple ‌at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/tsukuyomi/). ​The ‌restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ​— a ​description ‌computed from ​the displayed ​form ​itself. The ‌plain ​ASCII form ​*tsukuyomi* ​survives as ‌a ​modern convenience ‌imposed by ​the ‌early domain-name ​system; ‌the restoration, ‌not ​the fallback, ​is ​the form ​the project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Japanese ​characters as ​**月読**. ​Etymologically ​it means ‌"Moon ​reader"[^1].

​The ASCII ‌form ​*tsukuyomi* ‌survives only ​because ‌the ​early domain-name ​system ​could ​not carry ​diacritics; ‌it ​is a ‌technological ​compromise, ‌not an ​ancient ‌spelling. ​The Unicode ‌restoration ​**Tsukuyomi** ​recovers the ‌full ‌diacritic ‌detail of ​the ​scholarly ‌transliteration directly ​in ​the ‌address bar. ​The ​restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent form ​— ‌a ​description computed ​from ​the ​displayed form ‌itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

- ​**t** ​→ **T** ‌— ‌Same
- ‌**s** → ‌**s** ​— ‌Same
- **u** ​→ ​**u** ​— Same
- ‌**k** ​→ ​**k** — ​Same
- ‌**u** ​→ **u** ​— ​Same
- ‌**y** → ​**y** ‌— ​Same
- **o** ‌→ ​**o** ‌— Same
- ‌**m** ​→ ​**m** — ​Same
- ​**i** ‌→ **i** ‌— ​Same

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name ​is **/tsɯ.kɯ.jo.mi/** ​— Modern ​Standard ​Japanese (Hepburn).[^1]

​Phoneme by ‌phoneme:

- ​**Tsu-** — ​Voiceless alveolar ‌affricate ​[ts] plus ‌close back ​unrounded ‌[ɯ]; from ​月 'moon/month'
- ​**-ku-** ​— Voiceless ​velar stop ​[k] ‌plus close ​back ‌unrounded [ɯ]
- ​**-yo-** — ‌Palatal ​approximant [j] ‌plus open-mid ​[o]; ‌from 夜 ​'night' or ​読 ‌'to read/count'
- ‌**-mi** — ‌Bilabial ​[m] plus ​close front ‌[i]

​For the ​modern speaker, ‌the ​closest approximation ​is: 'TSOO-koo-yoh-mee' ‌— ​the initial ‌'ts' is ​crisp, ​and the ​final vowel ​is ‌clear.

Kindred ‌and historical ​forms ‌of the ​name:

- **Japanese** ​— ‌月読 (Tsukuyomi), ‌'Moon Reader' ‌or ‌'Moon Night' ​— yomi ‌may ​encode yomu, ​'to count ​the ‌months'
- **Siblings** ​— ​Amaterasu (sun) ​and Susanoo ‌(storms), ​born from ​Izanagi's misogi
- ​**Domain** ‌— The ​moon and ‌the ​night

Tsukuyomi ‌keeps its ​restoration ‌plain: plain ‌Hepburn. He ​is ​the moon ​god and ​sibling ‌of the ‌sun goddess ​Amaterasu.

domains.body:
**Tsukuyomi** ​is ‌the ‌moon kami ​of ​Japanese ​myth, ​born ​from Izanagi's ‌right ​eye ​when ‌the ​creator washed ‌away ​the ‌pollution ​of ​Yomi. He ​rules ​the ​night ‌and ​the counting ‌of ​months, ‌and ​his ‌entire narrative ​turns ‌on ​a ​single ‌act ‌of violence ‌that ​separated ​him ‌forever ​from the ​sun.[^1]

### ‌Moon ​God

​Ruler ‌of the ​night ‌sky ​and ​the ​lunar calendar ​that ‌numbers ‌the ​months.

### ‌Sibling of ​Amaterasu

​Born ‌with ‌her ‌from ‌Izanagi's purification ​— ‌the ​night's ​twin ​of the ‌day.

### ​Night ​Ruler

​He ‌governs the ​realm ​opposite ​the ‌sun, ​where nothing ‌ripens.

### ​Separated ‌Deity

​His ‌killing of ‌Uke-mochi ​divided ​him ​from ​Amaterasu into ‌day ‌and ​night.

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki 1 (variant birth accounts, the five grains).

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated with ‌Tsukuyomi ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small set ​of ‌recurring ​attributes, ​each ‌a compressed ​statement ‌about ​the ‌name:[^1]

- ​**Moon** — ​The ​luminous ​body ​he ‌rules; in ​court ‌poetry ​the ‌moon ​outshines every ‌other ​image ‌of ​the ​sky
- **Night** ‌— ‌The ‌dark ​half ​of the ‌cosmic ​day; ​his ‌estrangement ​from the ​sun ‌fixed ​its ‌boundary
- **Blade** ​— ​The ​weapon ​with ‌which he ‌answered ​Uke-mochi's ‌feast ​— ​purity's fatal ‌fastidiousness
- ‌**Crescent** ‌— ‌Waxing ​and waning; ‌the ​counting ​of ​months ‌that his ​name ​may ​encode
- ‌**The ​five grains** ​— ​Rice, ‌millet, ​beans, ‌wheat, and ​soy ‌born ​from ‌Uke-mochi's ‌slain body ​— ​food ​that ​his ‌night can ‌never ​ripen

mythology.body:
Tsukuyomi's mythology is the ​shortest dossier of the three celestial siblings, ‌and the chronicles themselves treat him as ‌an afterthought. What survives is **one birth, ​one killing, and one eternal estrangement** — enough ​to divide the sky.[^1]

### From the Right ​Eye of Izanagi (The Birth)

After his ​escape from Yomi, Izanagi washed away the ​pollution of the underworld, and the three ‌great sovereign deities came from his face: ​**Amaterasu** from the left eye, **Tsukuyomi** from ​the right eye, and **Susanoo** from the ‌nose (Kojiki 1). Izanagi appointed Amaterasu to ​rule the day and Tsukuyomi the night, dividing ‌the luminous and dark halves of the ​world between the siblings. Where Amaterasu received ‌her father's necklace and the highest heaven, ​Tsukuyomi received no emblem — a first ​hint of how thin his dossier would ​remain. His name joins tsuku, the moon, ​with yomi, read as 'night' or as ​'counting,' the deity who numbers the months. ‌The myth establishes the moon as the sun's ​twin: born in the same instant of ‌purification, ruling the complementary half of the ​sky.[^2]

### The Feast of Uke-mochi (The Killing)

‌Amaterasu heard of a wondrous goddess of ​food, Uke-mochi, and sent Tsukuyomi to look ‌upon her. Uke-mochi turned toward the land ​and from her mouth and body produced ‌a banquet — boiled rice, millet, and ​every grain (Kojiki 1). Tsukuyomi was revolted: a ​meal that issued from a body was ‌pollution itself, and he drew his blade ‌and killed her. Amaterasu's anger was immediate ‌and eternal — she declared him an ​evil god she would never again face, ​and from that moment the sun and ‌moon kept separate courses. From Uke-mochi's slain ​body the useful world sprang: silkworms from ​her head, rice from her eyes, millet from ‌her ears, beans from her nose, wheat ​and soy from her lower body (Nihon ​Shoki 1). The myth weighs purity against ‌fecundity: the moon's fastidious blade cuts the ​night off from the very source of ‌food.

### Why Sun and Moon Never Meet ​(The Separation)

The Kojiki gives no further ​adventures of Tsukuyomi — his entire narrative after ​the killing is one sentence of divine ​estrangement. Amaterasu, as sovereign of the day, ‌pronounced the sentence; the moon god departed, ‌and the chronicle lets him go without ​a shrine, a child, or another deed. ‌Later readers noticed the astronomy already inside ​the story: the moon that strikes down ​the goddess of food is the moon ‌that rules the night in which nothing grows; ‌the sun that refuses to see him ‌is the sun under whose gaze the ‌five grains ripened from Uke-mochi's body. The ​separation is thus both an eternal feud ‌and a daily rotation — estrangement written ​across the sky as the alternation of ​day and night, the celestial siblings meeting ​only at the thresholds of dawn and ‌dusk, and never face to face.

### A God ​at the Edge of the Record (The ​Variants)

The compilers of the Nihon Shoki ​reproduce several variant accounts of the celestial ‌birth, and their disagreements are themselves informative: ​the recensions differ in the occasion of ​the washing and in small details of ​order, and one tradition lets Tsukuyomi's name ‌be read as 'moon-counter,' the deity who ​numbers the months; the Kojiki grants him the ‌grand style Tsukuyomi-no-mikoto, 'His Augustness Moon-Night,' and ​then never uses it again. No variant ‌gives him a further myth. The scholarly ​conclusion is sober: unlike his siblings, Tsukuyomi ‌attracted no cycle of tales — perhaps, ‌as some have argued, because the moon's ​waxing and waning were read through other ​divinities in the popular cults. His faintness ​in the record is the most distinctive thing ​about him: the god of the night ‌keeps to the edges of the text, ‌exactly as the moon keeps to the ​edges of the day.

syncretism.body:
Tsukuyomi ​was drawn ‌early ‌into the ​Buddhist ​astronomy that ​mapped ​the pantheon ​onto ‌the heavens: ​in ​esoteric mandalas ‌the ​lunar deity ‌appears ​among the ‌devas ​as a ​moon-disc ​(gachirin), and ​medieval ​Shinto-Buddhist thought ‌quietly read ​the ‌moon kami ​as ‌Dainichi's reflected ​light ‌— the ​moon ‌as borrowed ​radiance, ​a natural ‌metaphor ‌for compassion ‌that ​mirrors its ​source. ‌In honji-suijaku ​terms ​he attracted ‌no ​major buddha ​of ‌his own, ​and ‌his cult ​shrank ​as Amaterasu's ​and ​Susanoo's grew. ‌His ‌afterlife is ​more ‌literary than ​liturgical: ​the moon ‌of ‌the Man'yōshū ‌and ‌the Kokinshū ​poems ‌is Tsukuyomi's ​territory ​whether named ​or ‌not.[^1]

Kindred ​figures in ​the ​PuniCodex cross-tradition ‌index ​include [[amaterasu|Amaterasu]] ​(sun-moon ​sibling rivalry), ‌[[susanoo|Susanō]] ​(storm and ‌moon ​siblings), [[artemis|Ártemis]] ‌(moon ​/ lunar), ‌[[change|Chángé]] ‌(moon / ​lunar), ​[[hati|Hati]] (moon ​/ ​lunar), and ‌[[hekate|Hekátē]] ‌(moon / ​lunar).

archaeology.body: Material ​evidence ‌for ‌Tsukuyomi ​is correspondingly ​scarce. ​His ​chief ​sanctuary, ‌the ​Tsukiyomi-no-miya, ​stands ‌among ​the subsidiary ‌shrines ​of ‌Ise ​and ​is ​renewed ​with ​the ‌Grand Shrine's ​twenty-year ‌rebuilding ​cycle; ‌a ​mirror ‌is ​enshrined ‌there ​as his ​body. ‌Heian ‌court ‌records ​document ​monthly ‌tsukimi ​rites ​— offerings ‌of ​dumplings, ​susuki ‌grass, ​and ‌sake ​to ​the harvest ​moon ​— ‌and ‌the ​Engishiki ‌lists ​him ​among ‌the kami ‌receiving ‌state ‌offerings. ​Beyond ‌Ise, ​independent ​shrines ​to ‌Tsukuyomi are ​rare, ​which ​historians ‌of ​religion ​read ​as ‌the ​material trace ‌of ​his ‌thin ​mythology: ‌a ‌deity ​with ​no ​narrative cycle ​attracted ‌no ‌pilgrimage ​geography.[^1]

meditation.body:
Tsukuyomi ​is the ‌study ‌of how ​little ​a god ​needs. No ​temple ​empire, no ‌epic, ​no miracles ​— ‌one birth, ​one ‌terrible act, ​one ‌sentence of ​exile, and ​the ​sky is ​arranged. ​Perhaps that ‌is ​why the ‌tradition ​did not ‌embroider ​him: the ‌moon asks ​for ‌no stories, ​because ​everyone looks ‌up ‌and supplies ‌their ​own.

His ​single ‌myth is ​a parable ​about ‌discernment gone ​rigid ​— a ‌purity ​that cannot ‌bear ​the body's ​generosity, ​and so ​murders the ‌goddess ‌who feeds ​the ‌world. The ​moonlit ​nights that ‌follow ‌are beautiful ‌and ‌infertile. To ​live wholly ‌by ​his light ​is ​to starve ‌in ​radiance; to ​live ​wholly by ‌the ​sun is ​to know ​nothing ‌of the ​night. ‌The myth ​of ‌the estranged ​siblings ‌keeps both ‌halves ​of the ​sky in ​one ​household — ‌divided, ‌but never ​divorced.[^1]
